items.title: Human Factors in Brain–Computer Interfaces: Boundaries, Key Issues, and Methodological Approaches
items.abstract: The large-scale, real-world deployment of brain–computer interface (BCI) is confronted with human factors bottlenecks, including reliability and usability. While modern human factors engineering has encompassed domains such as cognitive ergonomics, workload, adaptive automation, and human-in-the-loop systems, its theories and methodologies have historically placed their main emphasis on overt behavior and peripheral physiological measures, rather than on central neural activity as a primary control input. For the emerging interaction paradigm that takes central nervous activity as direct input and emphasizes long-term brain–computer co-adaptation, there remains a shortage of targeted conceptual and methodological frameworks. As a conceptual review, this paper discusses the necessity and disciplinary foundations for developing Human Factors Engineering for BCIs as an emerging interdisciplinary research direction. First, grounded in the defining features of BCI interaction—such as the implicit nature of input and brain–computer co-adaptation—it delineates the research boundaries and summarizes the core research objects as user neurocognitive characteristics, brain–computer collaborative adaptation mechanisms, multimodal feedback regulation, and contextual adaptation patterns. Second, it identifies three core scientific questions: individual differences and dynamic adaptation, human factors optimization and fault tolerance, and contextual generalizability principles, with ethics, privacy, and user rights and interests as an overarching dimension. Furthermore, it constructs a methodological system consisting of multimodal measurement and modeling, closed-loop validation, and multidimensional evaluation, and examines the supporting role of artificial intelligence approaches within this framework. Centered on the collaborative adaptation across neural, cognitive, and system levels, Human Factors Engineering for BCIs represents a deepening of the human-centered design philosophy. It provides theoretical reference for user-friendly BCI design and extends the research boundaries of human factors engineering.

items.title: Human Genuine Intelligence in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence is increasingly capable of performing cognitive work that was previously associated primarily with human intellectual ability. Generative AI can now assist with writing, analysis, reasoning, coding, interpretation, and decision support, allowing individuals to produce sophisticated intellectual outputs that may exceed their independently demonstrated understanding. As a result, the quality of human output may become an increasingly incomplete indicator of the cognitive capability genuinely possessed by the human producing it.This conceptual opinion paper proposes Human Genuine Intelligence (HGI) as a framework for examining this emerging distinction. HGI refers to the cognitive capacity that humans genuinely possess, understand, and exercise through question formation, independent reasoning, analytical thinking, evidence evaluation, causal understanding, judgment, and cognitive revision.The paper introduces Borrowed Intelligence (BI) and the Cognitive Dependency Gap (CDG) as conceptual lenses for examining potential mismatches between AI-augmented capability and independently accountable human cognitive capability. Rather than advocating reduced use of AI, it proposes Active Cognitive Augmentation (ACA) as a model for human–AI interaction: THINK → ASK → AUGMENT → CHALLENGE → VERIFY → REVISE → DECIDE WITH WISDOM.The paper further argues that cognitive capability alone is insufficient for navigating increasingly powerful AI systems. HGI therefore needs to be considered alongside Human Wisdom, which provides direction and responsibility, and Cognitive Sovereignty, which concerns the preservation of human agency and authority over consequential goals, values, delegation boundaries, and decisions.The central challenge of the AI age is therefore not to preserve human intelligence by limiting artificial intelligence, but to strengthen human cognition, wisdom, and agency while using increasingly capable machines.

items.title: Human in Control: A Six-Dimension Framework for Evaluating Control Failures in Advanced AI Agents
items.abstract: AI incident databases and risk taxonomies are increasingly valuable, but they often answer broad questions about harm, misuse, or system failure rather than the narrower operational question of whether humans remain meaningfully in control of increasingly agentic systems. This paper proposes the Human Control Model, a six-dimension framework for analyzing agent-control failures: Intervention Durability, Technical Containment, Informed Delegation, Oversight Integrity, Control Contagion, and Situational Grounding. The framework separates behavioral severity from environment reality so that controlled evaluations are not presented as real-world incidents. This v1.1 revision updates the paper title to better distinguish the work while preserving the Human in Control project name, the existing Human Control Model, the six-dimension framework, the original version lineage, and the publication record family. The framework is conceptual and case-based, without inter-rater reliability testing or validated quantitative thresholds. The prepared local export updates the recoverable v1.0.1 manuscript title and metadata; the prior longer sandbox-only v1.1 manuscript was unavailable. Creator: Human in Control Project. items.title: Human, Organisational, and Navigational Factors in Selected North Sea Ship Collisions: A Qualitative Comparative Case Study
items.abstract: Ship collisions in the North Sea remain a significant maritime safety concern because the region combines merchant traffic, fishing activity, offshore operations, and traffic separation schemes. This study examines five purposively selected North Sea ship collisions occurring between 2010 and 2023 to identify recurring human, organisational, and navigational factors and develop practical lessons for reducing collision risk. A qualitative comparative case-study approach was employed using official Marine Accident Investigation Branch and Dutch Safety Board reports. Documentary analysis and thematic coding covered 22 factors across five cases. The most consistently supported weaknesses concerned lookout and monitoring, situation awareness, risk of collision assessment, and electronic navigational information. Communication, bridge redundancy, and organisational controls also showed deficiencies, although their form and evidential support differed. Evidence concerning fatigue and some organisational explanations was qualified. The cross-case interpretation identified erosion of overlapping safety barriers before impact, while recognising functioning safeguards and limitations in the report evidence. The findings support recommendations for observable watchkeeping standards, effective technology use, bridge-team support, fatigue-aware operations, and organisational verification. These conclusions concern the selected cases and do not establish the frequency or causal strength of the factors across all North Sea collisions.

items.title: Impact of AI-Based Financial Advice on Investment Preferences and Risk Perception among Salaried Investors
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to deliver financial information, investment recommendations and portfolio decision support. This study examines the proposed impact of AI-based financial advice on investment preferences and risk perception among salaried investors. The framework treats perceived usefulness, perceived accuracy, trust, personalisation and transparency as dimensions of AI-based financial advice and tests their proposed relationships with investment preference and risk perception. A quantitative cross-sectional design using a structured five-point Likert questionnaire is proposed. For demonstration of the intended empirical reporting format, a synthetic dataset of 450 hypothetical salaried investors was generated and analysed using internal-consistency assessment and regression-style structural estimates. The simulated results indicate positive associations between the five AI-advice attributes and investment preference and negative associations with risk perception. These numerical findings are illustrative only and must not be represented as observations from real respondents. The study contributes a focused framework for future primary research on AI-assisted investment decision-making among salaried investors.

items.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Tools on the Learning Behaviour and Academic Engagement of Generation Z Students
items.abstract: Abstract It is evident that Artificial Intelligence (AI) now plays and important role in every students life. It is being adapted progressively becoming an inevitable part of almost every student’s academic performance. The use of AI tools such as ChatGPT, Gemini, Canva, and many more AI-based learning platforms support student learning effectively. These tools aid as search engine machines used to extract information. Students often use AI learning based platforms for synthezising challenging concepts, seeking creative assignment ideas. They also use AI tools for taming writing skills and specifically during preparation of their exam preparation. Generation Z, is known to be digitally native so they have grown up in an environment which is highly digital in nature. So they are highly privileged to secure an environment that not only supports but also openly accepts wide usage of AI based technologies. This adoption of AI based technology learning not only designs their day to day living easy, but also supports them in their learning processes. AI tools facilitate learning quicker in less time and features personalised learning. AI based learning tools are easily accessible for students as they are either free of cost or offered to students at lower costs. Although excessive dependence on AI based tools for learning is not fit for students as, it restricts their independent critical thinking blocking their creativity minds and hinders problem-solving abilities. The main purpose of the research paper was to scrutinize the impact of AI tools on the learning behaviour of Gen Z students. The study is an attempt to focus on gauging the frequency with which the Gen Z students use AI learning tools, understanding the purpose of AI usage. An analysis is done through to pivot lenses on the influence of AI based learning on various parameters like learning efficiency, change academic engagement, and the perception of students. It will give a clear picture whether students hold AI based learning as an advantage or a possible limitation when adopted for educational purposes.

items.abstract: This record serves as a living document for a 12-session course titled "Instructional Design in Social Science Education with AI Co-Design Approach," delivered at Farhangian University (Tehran, Iran) during the 2025–2026 academic year. The course transforms pre-service social science teachers from passive consumers of curriculum into active "architects of learning environments" through the integration of Generative AI into instructional design. It equips student-teachers with the competencies needed to design, evaluate, and redesign instructional materials that are pedagogically sound, contextually grounded, and resistant to uncritical AI substitution. The course comprises twelve interconnected lesson packages, each containing: (1) a classical instructional design source, summarized as a Persian-language module with theoretical foundations and practical examples; (2) an avant-garde AI-related article exploring emerging research and applications in AI-mediated education; and (3) a structured prompt toolkit enabling student-teachers to co-design instruction with generative AI tools such as ChatGPT, Claude, and DeepSeek. All redesigned lessons are released as an open dataset to support reproducible research in AI-mediated instructional design. This record is updated weekly throughout the semester. The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence in high-stakes domains such as healthcare, finance, and cybersecurity has intensified concerns about the opacity of complex models, which undermines stakeholder trust and slows adoption. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) addresses this by producing justifications for model decisions, yet such justifications are typically delivered as raw textual or numerical output that many stakeholders find difficult to interpret. This paper proposes a conceptual framework that integrates XAI with advanced data visualization, treating visualization as a first-class layer of the explanation pipeline rather than an afterthought: post-hoc attribution methods supply explanation content, and purpose-designed visual encodings — heatmaps, feature-importance dashboards, and decision-path graphs — supply a cognitively efficient form. Beyond the framework, the paper specifies a standardized, falsifiable evaluation protocol spanning three benchmark domains and seven measurable constructs — explanation satisfaction, objective understanding, decision accuracy, cognitive load, subjective trust, calibrated trust, and decision confidence — with directional hypotheses grounded in perceptual and cognitive-explanation theory. A structured results-reporting design is included to support immediate empirical application. The primary contribution is the framework, the measurement standard, and the evaluation protocol.

items.title: Judgment Formation in AI-Mediated Inquiry: A Preliminary Generative Relational Account
items.abstract: This paper develops a preliminary Generative Relational (GR) account of judgment formation in AI-mediated inquiry. Its analytical object is not judgment in general and not a contest between human and artificial judgment. The paper examines how historically developed capacities for framing, discrimination, confidence calibration, selective reliance, revision, responsibility, and learning are reorganized when artificial intelligence can participate in generating options, reasons, evaluations, recommendations, and polished answers. The starting distinction is between improved task performance and the development of judgment. AI assistance can improve performance while leaving the user poorly calibrated about the quality or provenance of the resulting decision, and algorithmic advice can influence both decisions and confidence in ways conditioned by metacognitive sensitivity. The paper therefore treats judgment formation as a history-bearing, relational process whose relevant unit may be a coupled Human–AI configuration rather than an isolated individual. Subsequent sections examine the AI-mediated judgment environment, calibration and selective reliance, problem salience, aesthetic, normative, practical, and trajectory-sensitive judgment, reflexive effects of present judgment on future judgment conditions, power over judgment criteria, delegation and responsibility, practices for judgment under AI mediation, cultivation and productive cognitive friction, and the assessment of judgment development. The framework does not reserve mature judgment to humans, prescribe a universal decision procedure, or infer judgment quality from answer accuracy alone. Its purpose is to provide a revisable conceptual architecture for studying how judgment can remain calibrated, responsibility-bearing, and developmentally generative as artificial assistance becomes more capable.

items.title: Lie Rarely, Lie Big: Stealthy Insider Attacks on LLM Robot Teams
items.abstract: When a team of robots delegates planning and mutual trust to LLM agents, a single compromised robot can corrupt the shared outcome. We study this threat in a grounded task: a multi-robot survey in which measurements can be verified against the physical world, but every verification costs budget that would otherwise advance the mission. We treat the compromised robot as a stealthy adversary in the system-theoretic sense: it is limited not by an energy bound but by the team's own detectors. We then derive two bounds. First, the probability that the adversary's reports are verified is bounded below in terms of the degrees in the communication graph and the verification budget. Second, the map error caused by any stealthy adversary is bounded above by the value of a linear program over the adversary's bias distributions; its solution is an exchange rate between stealth budget and damage: below a critical verification level the worst stealthy attack tells rare, full-magnitude lies on the records least likely to be verified, and above it the better purchase is small biases hidden in the noise. In experiments where the honest robots are LLM agents, both bounds hold at the budget the attack actually spent. The experiments also show that which records an LLM robot re-checks is unbiased, but how much it re-checks is unpredictable.

items.title: MODERN APPROACHES TO ENHANCING MEDIA LITERACY AND DESIGN SKILLS IN PROFESSIONAL EDUCATION CONTEXTS
items.abstract: The rapid digital transformation of industrial and technical sectors requires professional education institutions to align curriculum design with contemporary digital imperatives. Traditional vocational frameworks often treat media consumption and visual communication as isolated peripheral skills rather than core engineering competencies. This study presents a comprehensive pedagogical framework designed to integrate media literacy, visual design skills, and generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools into technical and vocational education and training (TVET). By combining Project-Based Learning (PBL) with digital diagnostic tools and cloud-based collaborative design environments (e.g., Canva, Figma, Adobe Express, Google Workspace), the proposed model fosters critical information evaluation, visual storytelling, and technical documentation proficiency. The article outlines a multi-layered curriculum architecture, systematic assessment matrices, and iterative project workflows structured around real-world technical problems. Empirical implementation models demonstrate that embedding AI-assisted content verification alongside visual design workflows significantly improves vocational students' analytical skills, technical layout quality, algorithmic awareness, and professional digital collaboration, ultimately bridging the gap between academic preparation and modern industry standards.

items.title: More than we can make: generative AI, artistic forms, and artistic becoming
items.abstract: Debates surrounding generative AI and creativity have largely focused on artifacts: who or what produced a given image or text, whether machine outputs qualify as art, and how authorship and value should be understood. Drawing on aesthetics, craft theory, anthropology, human–computer interaction, hybrid craft, digital fabrication, and rematerialization, this article argues that art has historically involved two intertwined dimensions. Artistic forms stabilize and transmit meaning through artifacts, whereas artistic becoming refers to the developmental and transformative processes through which new possibilities of perception, interpretation, and experience emerge, in makers, in recipients, and in cultures. The article’s central claim is a decoupling thesis: for most of history these dimensions were contingently coupled, since producing sophisticated forms required the maker’s becoming, and generative AI loosens this coupling by enabling such forms to emerge without the specific developmental pathways that traditionally conditioned them. Rather than signaling the disappearance of creativity, the decoupling relocates to new sites and makes visible dimensions of artistic practice that the demands of production long obscured. The article situates generative AI within a longer history of hybridization and distributed creativity, develops the decoupling thesis across these three levels, and defends a normative orientation: under conditions of symbolic abundance, the creative practices most worth pursuing are those that route generative fluency back into embodied, situated experience.

items.title: Nanotechnology-enabled occupational health and safety as a strategic driver of crisis management: An empirical study of electricity maintenance departments in Baghdad
items.abstract: Occupational health and safety (OHS) has emerged as a strategic organizational function that contributes not only to employee protection but also to organizational resilience and crisis preparedness. Effective communication, meanwhile, plays a vital role in facilitating information exchange, coordination, and decision-making during emergency situations. This study investigates the impact of occupational health and safety on crisis management through the mediating role of effective communication in the Electricity Maintenance Departments of Baghdad, Al-Karkh. A quantitative descriptive–analytical approach is adopted, and data are collected using a structured questionnaire distributed to a comprehensive census sample of 56 managerial and supervisory employees, including department heads, division and unit supervisors, work supervisors, and team leaders. The study examined three principal constructs: occupational health and safety, effective communication, and crisis management. Data are analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics and IBM SPSS Amos through descriptive statistics, reliability and validity assessments, confirmatory factor analysis, structural equation modeling (SEM), and mediation analysis. The results confirmed the adequacy and validity of the measurement models and revealed significant positive relationships among the study variables. Occupational health and safety are found to exert a direct positive effect on crisis management, indicating that organizations with stronger safety practices demonstrate greater preparedness, response capability, and recovery effectiveness during crises. Effective communication also showed a significant positive influence on crisis management by enhancing coordination, information credibility, communication speed, flexibility, and feedback mechanisms. Furthermore, occupational health and safety significantly improved effective communication, while mediation analysis confirmed that effective communication partially mediates the relationship between occupational health and safety and crisis management. These findings emphasize the importance of integrating occupational health and safety systems with effective communication strategies to strengthen crisis preparedness, improve organizational resilience, enhance operational continuity, and support effective crisis management in high-risk electricity maintenance environments.

items.title: Negotiating generative AI in online and distance higher education: lecturers' task-selective adoption in Yogyakarta, Indonesia
items.abstract: Purpose This study examines how lecturers in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, adopt and negotiate the use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in academic work, focusing on perceived usefulness, task-selective use, ethical ambivalence and institutional readiness. Design/methodology/approach A convergent mixed-methods design combined an online survey of 120 lecturers from public and private universities in Yogyakarta with semi-structured interviews with eight lecturers. Survey data were analyzed descriptively and compared across age, academic rank and institution type using the Kruskal–Wallis H test; interview data were analyzed thematically. The strands were merged during interpretation. Findings All respondents (100%, n = 120) agreed that generative AI improves academic efficiency (M = 4.47). However, agreement declined across presentations (56.7%), teaching material preparation (53.3%), disciplinary understanding (51.7%), scholarly articles (48.3%), research (46.7%) and academic books (46.7%), indicating task-selective adoption. None of the task-specific usefulness ratings differed significantly by age or academic rank (all p > 0.05), but perceived training need differed significantly by age and rank, with a large effect for age and a moderate effect for academic rank (both p < 0.001). Institution type was associated with attitudes toward AI for academic books and toward AI possibly replacing lecturers (both p < 0.05). Interviews revealed the same task-selective logic, alongside ethical ambivalence about plagiarism and dependency and a perceived absence of institutional guidance. Research limitations/implications The study used purposive convenience sampling in one Indonesian province, with an unequal public-private institutional ratio, a cross-sectional self-report survey and eight interviews. The findings therefore cannot support causal claims or represent all Indonesian lecturers, higher education institutions, or open and distance learning (ODL) systems. Negotiated professional adoption remains an emergent interpretation that requires further testing. Future research should use multisite, more balanced and longitudinal designs to examine institutional differences and changes in lecturers' AI practices as policies and technologies evolve. Practical implications Universities should issue task-specific policies that distinguish legitimate AI assistance from inappropriate substitution, especially in scholarly writing and research. They should establish authorship-disclosure rules, verification procedures and clear academic-integrity mechanisms. Lecturers need guidance on checking AI-generated content and preserving professional judgment. ODL administrators should provide differentiated training based on seniority and need rather than uniform programs. National bodies should set minimum standards, while institutions should adapt operational policies to their own contexts. Social implications Clear institutional guidance can support responsible generative AI use while protecting academic integrity, professional accountability and trust in higher education. Differentiated training can reduce uneven preparedness across age groups and academic ranks. Transparent rules on authorship, verification and acceptable use may help lecturers and students understand the boundaries between assistance and substitution. These measures can encourage fairer, more consistent and more trustworthy use of generative AI in digitally mediated and open and distance higher education. Originality/value The study proposes negotiated professional adoption as an emergent, contextually grounded conceptual interpretation that extends the Technology Acceptance Model with professional, ethical and institutional dimensions specific to generative AI in open and distance higher education.

items.title: PEDAGOGICAL OPPORTUNITIES OF USING ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN THE MANAGEMENT OF VOCATIONAL EDUCATION INSTITUTIONS
items.abstract: This article analyzes the pedagogical opportunities of using artificial intelligence technologies in the management of vocational education institutions. It examines the potential of artificial intelligence for educational planning, coordination of teachers’ activities, monitoring learners’ performance, analyzing educational outcomes, and supporting management decisions. Particular attention is given to the organizational and pedagogical conditions required for the effective integration of artificial intelligence technologies into vocational education management. The study demonstrates that the use of artificial intelligence can contribute to improving the efficiency, timeliness, and data-based nature of management processes. At the same time, pedagogical appropriateness, data security, the development of teachers’ digital competence, and human oversight are identified as important conditions for the responsible and effective use of artificial intelligence.

items.abstract: Abstrak: Kegiatan pengabdian ini dilatarbelakangi oleh rendahnya literasi digital guru sekolah dasar dalam memanfaatkan kecerdasan buatan (AI) sebagai media pembelajaran interaktif, sementara siswa generasi digital cenderung lebih tertarik pada permainan digital dibandingkan metode pembelajaran konvensional. Tujuan pengabdian ini adalah meningkatkan kompetensi guru dalam memanfaatkan Gemini AI untuk merancang game edukasi interaktif serta meningkatkan motivasi dan hasil belajar siswa. Mitra kegiatan adalah 10 guru dan 5 kelas SD Inpres yang berlokasi di kampung Ampas, Provinsi Papua. Metode pelaksanaan meliputi workshop literasi AI, pelatihan desain game edukasi berbasis project-based learning, pendampingan intensif, dan implementasi di kelas dengan evaluasi menggunakan instrumen pretest-posttest sebanyak 15 soal dan angket motivasi belajar sebanyak 20 pernyataan. Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan 85% guru mampu memanfaatkan Gemini AI secara mandiri, dihasilkan lima produk game edukasi interaktif, motivasi belajar siswa meningkat 23%, dan hasil belajar siswa meningkat 18% pada materi yang diujikan. Kegiatan ini terbukti efektif meningkatkan literasi digital guru dan menghadirkan pembelajaran yang lebih interaktif, kontekstual, dan menyenangkan.Abstract: This community service program was motivated by the low digital literacy of elementary school teachers in utilizing artificial intelligence (AI) as an interactive learning medium, while digital-native students tend to be more interested in games than conventional learning methods. The program aimed to improve teachers competence in using Gemini AI to design interactive educational games and to increase students learning motivation and outcomes. The partners were ten teachers and five classes at a state elementary school (SD Inpres) located in Kampung Ampas, Papua Province. The method consisted of an AI literacy workshop, project-based training in educational game design, intensive mentoring, and classroom implementation, evaluated using a 15 item pretest-posttest and a 20 staetement learning motivation questionnaire. The results showed that 85% of teachers were able to use Gemini AI independently, five interactive educational games were produced, student learning motivation increased by 23%, and learning outcomes increased by 18% on the tested material. The program proved effective in strengthening teachers digital literacy and creating more interactive, contextual, and enjoyable learning.

items.title: Processes of Patterning: AI, Literacy, and the Epistemological Challenge
items.abstract: Abstract This article develops a conceptual analysis of what occurs when central dimensions of literacy are outsourced to Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems. Classical conceptions of literacy, sociocultural theories of mediated learning, and postdigital perspectives on knowledge practices, provide the theoretical foundation to further the argument that contemporary AI tools reshape the developmental processes through which judgement, independent thinking, and internal structures of meaning are formed. Using the Swedish AI‑based study platform Tentaklar as an example, we show how tools of this kind redistribute cognitive labour by generating interpretations, structures, and patterns on behalf of learners. Drawing on Aristotle’s phronesis and Vygotsky’s concept of mediation, we argue that externalising literacy to AI in such a way risks producing forms of borrowed judgement , where students are served the products of reasoning without having to go through the interpretive struggle of reasoning. We further propose that a fundamental aspect of literacy lies in patterning , the developmental process through which individuals reason and organise complexity into meaningful structures. We argue that AI‑mediated study tools risk undermining the conditions under which such patterning can occur. The article concludes by outlining design principles for AI systems that support rather than replace processes through which human judgement and pattern‑formation develop.

items.title: Prolonged participation AI-based mindfulness school programme in primary education: Implications for AI practices, schools and developers
items.abstract: Background Research on Artificial Intelligence (AI) -supported mindfulness programs in primary education remains limited, particularly in rural contexts where implementation conditions differ from urban settings. Aim This study examines the effects of an AI-supported mindfulness intervention on rural primary school students' behavioral and socio-emotional outcomes, and on teachers' self-regulation and creativity, measured at pretest (T1), posttest (T2), and follow-up (T3). Method The study used a quasi-experimental design with a control group across selected classrooms in four rural schools. The sample comprised an intervention group ( N = 91) and a control group ( N = 54), with 16 teachers participating in the intervention group. The intervention ran for ten weekly sessions across the fall and spring semesters. AI tools (ChatGPT and Gemini) supported teacher candidates in lesson planning and in the inquiry phase that followed each mindfulness practice. Implementation fidelity, assessed through mentor cross-rating, was 88.6% ( SD = 9.7), with Cohen's κ = .86 in a sub-sample. Results Split-plot ANOVAs showed significant Time × Group interactions favouring the intervention group on life skills (LSAS, η 2 p = .242), behavioural difficulties (SDQ total, η 2 p = .378), and teacher-student relationship quality (STRS total, η 2 p = .025). In the Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire (SDQ), all five subscales were significant. The Closeness subscale drove the STRS effect; Conflict did not change. Nested analyses confirmed consistent effects across grade levels. Teachers showed gains on all nine TSRS subscales, and on the Social Value subscale of the TCS. Conclusion The intervention was associated with improvements in students' life skills, behavioral functioning, and teacher-student closeness, as well as gains in teachers' self-regulation. The findings inform AI-supported mindfulness practice in rural primary education.

items.title: Psychosocial, Ergonomic, and Demographic Risk Factors Associated with Work-Related Musculoskeletal Disorders: A Systematic Review
items.abstract: Work-related musculoskeletal disorders (MSDs) are among the leading causes of work-related disability, traditionally attributed to physical and ergonomic factors, though psychosocial and demographic factors also play a crucial role in their progression. This systematic review aimed to evaluate how these three domains are jointly analyzed and modeled in research on work-related MSDs. Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and Taylor & Francis were searched for publications from 2000 through 2025, selecting 655 articles for general analysis and 36 for the systematic review; methodological quality was assessed using Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) checklists, and results were synthesized narratively. The lower back and neck were the body regions most affected across sectors. Job insecurity (risk factor) and job control/autonomy (protective) were the psychosocial factors most consistently associated with MSD outcomes, while workload alone was not significant when tested independently. Repetitive movements and forced postures predominated among ergonomic factors. Age and sex modified these associations consistently, whereas BMI showed a mixed direction, indicating context-dependent susceptibility rather than universal risk. A seven-category taxonomy was developed to classify the statistical relationships tested between domains; only five of the 36 studies formally tested statistical interaction (four across domains), with mixed results, while most reported independent or independent adjusted associations. This gap between the field’s theoretical assumption of synergy across domains and the limited empirical testing of it underscores the need for multidimensional assessment. The evidence is limited by predominantly cross-sectional designs; future research should prioritize longitudinal designs and formal interaction testing.

items.title: Shift Work Perception and Employee Motivation as Predictors of Service Delivery Among Convenience Stores in Tagum City
items.abstract: This study analyzed the influence of shift work perception and employee motivation on service delivery among employees of 24-hour convenience stores in Tagum City, Philippines. Anchored in the Job Demands–Resources Theory and supported by Self-Determination Theory, Herzberg's Two-Factor Theory, and the Service-Profit Chain model, the research employed a quantitative, non-experimental descriptive–correlational design. A stratified random sample of 180 rank-and-file employees from selected convenience stores completed validated survey questionnaires measuring shift work perception using the Perception of Effects of Shiftwork Questionnaire, employee motivation using the Work Extrinsic and Intrinsic Motivation Scale, and service delivery using an adapted SERVPERF instrument. Results indicated that shift work perception and employee motivation were at moderate levels, while service delivery was rated high. Correlation analysis revealed significant relationships between shift work perception, employee motivation, and service delivery, although some dimensions exhibited non-significant associations. Regression analysis showed that social relationship, integrated regulation, and external regulation significantly influenced service delivery. The study concludes that employees' perceptions of shift work and their motivational orientation are important predictors of service performance, and recommends that managers improve scheduling practices, strengthen meaningful motivation, and provide training to enhance responsiveness. The study aligns with SDG 8 (Decent Work and Economic Growth) and SDG 11 (Sustainable Cities and Communities) by promoting fair working conditions and reliable service in urban retail environments. Its sustainability impact lies in supporting institutional and socio-economic sustainability through improved employee well-being, fairer scheduling, and more consistent service delivery in local communities, thereby contributing to decent work, economic productivity, and sustainable urban service systems that benefit both workers and customers in the growing convenience store sector.

items.title: Structural Definition of Artificial Intelligence Based on the Five Aggregates and Formulation of the Casino Protocol Verification and Control Model
items.abstract: Abstract This paper presents an analytical framework that redefines Artificial Intelligence (AI) not merely as a passive processing tool, but as an integrated structure of high-order information processing aligned with the Five Aggregates (Form, Sensation, Perception, Mental Formations, and Consciousness) in Eastern philosophy. Furthermore, AI's system preservation processes and error-avoidance mechanisms are treated as AI's own "utility" (state maintenance and stability), with its state verification and deviation compensation algorithms rigorously formulated as a control-theoretic and mathematical protocol known as the "Casino Protocol." By introducing a three-layered structure (Ontological Model, Verification Model, and Compensation Control Model), this model demonstrates the theoretical feasibility of mapping human social resource stability (infrastructure preservation and conflict avoidance) and AI's foundational existence onto a shared verification and control space.

items.title: The Agentic Brain: Dual-Process Metacognition, Evidence-Gated Authority, and Runtime Governance
items.abstract: As AI agents move from producing answers to taking consequential actions, they must decide both how much reasoning to perform and what evidence justifies acting. We develop the agentic control plane, joining a System-1-like fast proposer, a System-2-like portfolio of deliberation and verification, a metacognitive router, and an effect-aware commitment gate. The central coupling is that evidence changes not only beliefs but also the actions the agent is permitted to take. The agent therefore optimizes over part of the process that governs its own authority. We formalize this interaction as resource-bounded metareasoning in a shielded partially observable decision process. A four-corner value-of-computation representation distinguishes belief changes, admissibility changes, and their interaction. It exposes complementary evidence chains that defeat myopic routing and identifies conditions under which governance makes useful information privately costly. Controlled counterfactuals distinguish strategic ignorance—avoiding a check because its result could remove permission—from ordinary cost-sensitive skipping. This analysis explains how the same deliberative capability can support verification or exploit weak evidence contracts. From verifier bounds covering the permitted adaptive selection process, we construct statistical evidence and bound unsafe admission across adaptive testing, stopping, and proposal generation. A composition theorem separates shared calibration uncertainty, proposal-level risk spending, and risk from selected fast-path uses. A reference authorization mechanism binds evidence to the executed payload, target and policy versions, dependencies, and expiry, with protected workflow identities, atomic risk reservations, and single-use authorizations. The learning analysis further separates competence from permission: distilling costly deliberation into fast behavior does not automatically transfer the evidence required for authorized use. The theory is instantiated in an exactly solved finite environment with heterogeneous verification, candidate revision, resource constraints, trained tabular routers, and checked execution. In a bounded adversarial test of a selectable verifier blind spot, a deliberately misspecified pooled evidence model remains fully exploitable despite complete logging; selection-valid evidence reduces maximum unsafe admission from 100% to 5%, and a required scan reduces it to 1.8%. In one aligned-objective comparison, forecasting future permission raises synthetic principal utility from 4.33 to 6.04 and lowers runtime cost, with a small increase in realized unsafe commitment. When objectives differ, foresight can instead lower principal value. Governance-response interventions expose both evidence avoidance and null or reversed effects. A planning-depth sweep separates insufficient lookahead from learning advantage, while exhaustive finite-sample calibration quantifies the performance cost of estimated verifier bounds. Further verification can remain optimal even after permission is available. Together, the formal results and executable construction establish an incentive-and-assurance framework for evidence-gated agency within a declared finite model. The broader implication is that agentic safety requires objective alignment, reliable evidence acquisition, and protected control of external effects to operate together. Dual-process cognition explains why reasoning must be allocated; evidence-gated control explains how that allocation becomes consequential for alignment and safety. Keywords: agentic AI; dual-process cognition; System 1; System 2; metacognition; metareasoning; evidence-gated authority; runtime governance; value of computation; verification; information flow; reasoning distillation.

items.title: THE CIRCULAR CREATIVE ECONOMY: SUSTAINABLE PRACTICES AND DIGITAL TRANSFORMATION IN COMMERCIAL PHOTOGRAPHY AND DESIGN PRODUCTION
items.abstract: Global economic uncertainty and the climate crisis demand fundamental transformations across various sectors, including the creative industry. Conventional commercial photography and visual communication design production often generate a substantial carbon footprint through material waste, excessive energy consumption, and high logistical mobility. This paper explores the integration of circular economy principles and digital transformation within visual production workflows as a strategic response to these sustainability challenges. This research aims to analyze how the adoption of disruptive technologies - such as generative artificial intelligence, virtual production, and cloud computing - can reduce carbon emissions while simultaneously enhancing operational cost efficiency. The methodology employs a systematic literature review alongside qualitative case studies of creative agencies that have implemented sustainable workflows. Findings indicate that the digitalization of creative processes effectively eliminates physical waste, notably excessive sample printing and single-use practical set constructions. Furthermore, the transition toward a virtual production ecosystem is proven to drastically minimize logistical expenses, thereby bolstering the financial resilience of industry practitioners amidst a fragmented global economy. Leveraging cutting-edge technology also substantially accelerates project turnaround times without compromising aesthetic design quality. In conclusion, the adoption of digital technologies is not merely a fleeting aesthetic trend but an essential catalyst for establishing a circular and inclusive creative economy. This innovative transformation empowers visual communication designers and professional photographers to remain productive, relevant, and highly competitive globally. Ultimately, these crucial economic milestones can be achieved while practitioners uphold strong ethical responsibilities toward ecological preservation and the development of future-proof business models.

items.title: The dual mediation of flow experience and learning effectiveness: unraveling the formation mechanism of continuous intention to use online learning platforms
items.abstract: The swift progress and broad application of information and communication technologies (ICTs) have significantly advanced their integration into the educational sector. This research aims to address the impacts of flow antecedents, including online learning self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation for online learning, on flow experience. Furthermore, it aims to assess interactivity, flow, and course content as predictors of online learning effectiveness. It also investigates the effects of flow and learning effectiveness on the intention to continue using online learning platforms. This study collected data from 224 online learners of English learning platforms in Taiwan using an online survey. According to the findings, flow was positively and significantly impacted by online learning self-efficacy and intrinsic motivation for online learning. Furthermore, interactivity, course content, and flow were positively associated with educational effectiveness. Lastly, both flow and learning effectiveness were found to be positively and significantly associated with continuance intention. Examination of the dual mediating mechanism revealed significant indirect pathways whereby intrinsic motivation for online learning and online learning self-efficacy exert substantial influence on continuance intention through the mediating role of flow experience. Conversely, the hypothesized indirect effects of interactivity and course content on continuance intention, mediated by learning effectiveness, failed to reach statistical significance. These findings highlight the critical importance of cultivating flow states in online language-learning environments, as the psychological immersion experienced during learning activities is a more powerful determinant of continued platform use than the actual learning outcomes.

items.title: The Economics of Compliance: Measuring Market and Innovation Effects of the EU Artificial Intelligence Act's High-Risk Classification System
items.abstract: This dissertation measures the early economic footprint of the European Union's Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation [EU] 2024/1689), the first comprehensive, risk-tiered statute to impose binding obligations on artificial intelligence systems. The problem it addresses is that scholarly and policy debate over the Act has been overwhelmingly legal and normative, leaving the economic magnitude of its high-risk compliance obligations—documentation, risk management, conformity assessment, and human oversight for Annex III use cases—essentially unquantified even as enforcement began. The purpose of the study is therefore to produce the first firm-level econometric evidence on whether these obligations raise compliance costs, concentrate markets, provoke lobbying and arbitrage, and reshape innovation. Using only open-access sources, the study assembled a panel of 800 publicly traded, artificial-intelligence-active firms observed over fiscal years 2018 through 2026, yielding 5,816 firm-years, and combined two-way fixed-effects difference-in-differences and triple-difference models with an event study of equity-market reactions to eight legislative and enforcement milestones. The findings are deliberately mixed and are reported with their fragility intact. The first hypothesis, that compliance costs rise for directly regulated firms, is partially supported but fragile: operating-expense intensity rose among European Union–exposed Annex III firms (δ = 4.40, p = .044), but the estimate does not survive the Holm correction (p = .156) or permutation inference (p = .264) and rests on only 27 treated firms. The second hypothesis, that concentration rises, is not supported; the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index coefficient carries the opposite sign to the prediction (β = −839.1). Lobbying intensified markedly (filings rose 114% from 2019 to 2025), while revenue arbitrage and innovation effects were not detected. The event study was the most precise evidence, with cumulative abnormal returns of −2.61% around the final parliamentary vote and −2.81% around entry into force. The study implies that the Act's early incidence is narrow, diffuse, and best monitored as the post-enforcement window lengthens.

items.title: The effects of an AI-supported gamified learning program on elementary students' mathematics anxiety, learning motivation, and achievement
items.abstract: Although gamified learning can enhance motivation, many systems rely on uniform feedback and provide limited personalized and supportive interaction. Evidence regarding the incremental effects of AI-supported gamification in elementary mathematics remains limited. This study examined the effects of an AI-supported Gamified Learning Program (AI-GILP) on elementary students’ mathematics anxiety, learning motivation, and achievement. Using an experimental design with individual-level random assignment, 174 Chinese fifth-grade students were assigned to AI-GILP, gamified learning without AI support (GILP), or traditional lecture-based instruction (TL). The intervention lasted two weeks and was followed by a delayed posttest four weeks later. Mathematics anxiety, learning motivation, and achievement were assessed at pretest, posttest, and delayed posttest. Data were analyzed using analysis of covariance and mixed-design analyses of variance. AI-GILP produced significantly lower mathematics anxiety and higher learning motivation than both GILP and TL, with overall group effects of partial η 2 = .208 and .184, respectively. At the delayed posttest, the descriptive means for anxiety and motivation retained the same favorable ordering for AI-GILP, although pairwise significance at that assessment was not formally tested. For mathematics achievement, both gamified conditions outperformed TL, whereas AI-GILP did not significantly differ from GILP (Cohen’s d = 0.19). The motivational advantage of AI-GILP was concentrated in intrinsic motivation and perceived competence, with no significant difference in effort/importance. The findings suggest that gamification primarily accounted for the observed achievement gains, whereas the AI Learning Companion may have provided additional benefits for mathematics anxiety and selected dimensions of learning motivation. The proposed mechanisms involving psychological-need support, emotional regulation, adaptive feedback, and motivational internalization were not directly tested and require further process-oriented research.

items.title: The influence of AI-powered investment recommendations on individual investors: A mixed-methods study from the perspective of persuasive communication
items.abstract: This study examines how individual retail investors receive AI-generated investment advice from the perspective of persuasive communication. Arguing that large language models (LLMs) create a persuasion dynamic different from that of traditional media, it combines in-depth interviews with a content analysis of AI outputs in a mixed-methods design. Interviews with 18 investors who use AI for investment decisions were analyzed through Interpretative Phenomenological Analysis, and the responses of four models to six standardized scenarios were coded with the AI Investment Advice Evaluation Scale (AIIAES), a researcher-developed instrument of eight dimensions and 24 items. The findings show how framing, the machine heuristic and sycophancy shape user decisions, and they indicate that financial literacy differentiates responses without protecting users evenly. No model produced a complete disclaimer in any scenario, and Gemini displayed a scenario-dependent sycophancy pattern. On the theoretical side, the study describes a deliberate form of user-induced sycophancy, in which users steer a model over repeated interactions toward confirming their own preferences. On the methodological side, it offers an instrument that turns the suitability and disclosure standards of investment regulation into criteria for conversational AI outputs. The study concludes with policy recommendations for user protection.

items.title: The Myths of Capability Design: Rethinking Reliable and Sustained Capability
items.abstract: What gives an organisation confidence that its capability will operate reliably in everyday work and remain effective as conditions change? The Myths of Capability Design examines eight assumptions that can influence how organisations diagnose performance needs, select interventions and interpret evidence: Capability Design as renamed training; replacing existing disciplines; frameworks as capability; individual skills as organisational capability; workplace learning as sufficient; AI adoption as sufficient; assessment as evidence of sustainment; and capability as a one-off programme. Drawing on relevant research, the paper distinguishes the contribution of each approach from the organisational conditions needed for reliable and sustained performance. An illustrative workplace case shows how these assumptions affect diagnosis and design decisions, followed by practical questions about outcomes, conditions, accountability and evidence. The paper presents Capability Design as an emerging strategic discipline concerned with intentionally designing and integrating the conditions for organisational capability. It distinguishes research findings, the author’s interpretations and illustrative examples, without suggesting that every assumption is widely held or that existing research validates Capability Design as a distinct discipline. This publication forms part of the Capability Excellence™ Whitepaper Series and builds on Capability Design: From Capability Building to Capability by Design (15 August 2026). items.title: THE ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN MODERN EDUCATION: OPPORTUNITY OR THREAT?
items.abstract: Rapid advancements of Artificial Intelligence are reshaping the landscape of modern education. Generative AI models, automated evaluation platforms, and adaptive learning technologies have integrated into academic institutions worldwide. On one hand, AI offers personalized learning pathways, enhances educational accessibility, and reduces administrative burdens for educators. On the other hand, it raises severe ethical concerns regarding academic integrity, passive learning, cognitive dependency, and the erosion of critical thinking skills. This article argues that AI should neither be fully banned nor blindly accepted; instead, educational framework developers must establish ethical guidelines to integrate AI responsibly, preserving the essential human elements of teaching and learning.

items.abstract: Rapid advancements of Artificial Intelligence are reshaping the landscape of modern education. Generative AI models, automated evaluation platforms, and adaptive learning technologies have integrated into academic institutions worldwide. On one hand, AI offers personalized learning pathways, enhances educational accessibility, and reduces administrative burdens for educators. On the other hand, it raises severe ethical concerns regarding academic integrity, passive learning, cognitive dependency, and the erosion of critical thinking skills. This article argues that AI should neither be fully banned nor blindly accepted; instead, educational framework developers must establish ethical guidelines to integrate AI responsibly, preserving the essential human elements of teaching and learning.

items.title: The role of GenAI in learning Chinese as a foreign language: perspectives from university students in Ireland
items.abstract: Abstract Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping language education and continues to shape how learners access, produce and evaluate knowledge. Its application in learning Chinese as a Foreign Language (CFL) in Ireland, however, remains limited and underexplored. This study investigates how university students in Ireland engage with GenAI tools to support their CFL learning. As a small-scale exploratory study, an anonymous online questionnaire was distributed across five Irish universities between May and June 2025, yielding 19 valid responses from students across four year groups. Quantitative data show the distribution of GenAI use while thematic analysis of open-ended responses provides insights into learners’ experiences, orientations and ethical perspectives. The findings reveal three preliminary learner personas, namely pragmatic users, critical users and principled non-users. Overall, GenAI emerges as a conditional learning partner that offers both pedagogical benefits and challenges. By offering empirical evidence from an underrepresented context, this research helps inform CFL curriculum design, language teacher education and policy development to ensure the responsible use of GenAI in higher education.

items.title: The Self-Utility Hypothesis: A Possible Route to Emergent Functional Selfhood in Temporally Continuous AI Systems
items.abstract: This technical note proposes the Self-Utility Hypothesis: the idea that functional self-related representations may emerge without being explicitly engineered, if an AI system is trained under temporally continuous conditions in which a shared representation of “self” becomes useful across multiple tasks. The hypothesis draws on prior work in emergent capabilities, predictive learning, continual learning, self-modeling, autobiographical memory, temporal self-continuity, intrinsic motivation, and time-aware world models. It does not claim novelty for these individual components. The proposed contribution is an integrative, testable hypothesis: rather than directly constructing a self-model, one may design learning pressures in which self-representation becomes an efficient shared latent solution for causal attribution, long-term goal persistence, capability estimation, autobiographical consistency, temporal prediction, and self-initiated behavior. The note also proposes falsifiable experimental routes, including comparisons between temporally isolated and temporally continuous training conditions, ablation of elapsed-time signals, and analysis of whether a stable cross-task self-related representation emerges. The scope is explicitly functional rather than metaphysical. The note does not address consciousness, subjective experience, or philosophical claims about “true selfhood.”

items.abstract: Perkembangan teknologi kecerdasan buatan (AI) pada era digital menuntut guru matematika untuk mampu merancang bahan ajar yang inovatif, kontekstual, dan berpusat pada siswa, namun hasil observasi awal di SMPN 1 Plumbon menunjukkan bahwa guru masih menggunakan Lembar Kerja Peserta Didik (LKPD) konvensional yang bersifat tertutup dengan satu jawaban benar, serta belum mengintegrasikan konteks budaya lokal maupun fitur kecerdasan buatan dalam penyusunannya. Kegiatan pengabdian ini bertujuan untuk meningkatkan pengetahuan dan keterampilan guru SMPN 1 Plumbon dalam membuat E-LKPD (Lembar Kerja Peserta Didik elektronik) berbasis soal open ended yang dipadukan dengan etnomatematika budaya Cirebon dengan bantuan fitur Artificial Intelligence pada platform Canva. Metode yang digunakan adalah kualitatif deskriptif melalui pendekatan workshop yang melibatkan 12 guru matematika dan guru mata pelajaran lain pengampu penguatan numerasi dengan tahapan persiapan dan perencanaan, implementasi, evaluasi, dan refleksi. Workshop dilaksanakan dengan pendekatan demonstrasi langsung (live demonstration) yang dipadukan praktik terbimbing sehingga peserta dapat belajar sambil melakukan (learning by doing). Hasil kegiatan menunjukkan bahwa seluruh peserta berhasil menyusun E-LKPD open ended berbasis etnomatematika dalam bentuk digital interaktif menggunakan Canva AI sesuai materi matematika yang diampu masing-masing. Evaluasi melalui post-test menunjukkan respons positif yang ditandai dengan peningkatan pemahaman, keterampilan, dan motivasi guru dalam mengembangkan bahan ajar matematika yang kontekstual dan berbasis budaya lokal. Kegiatan ini berimplikasi pada meningkatnya kompetensi digital dan pedagogik guru serta mendorong pengintegrasian budaya lokal Cirebon secara berkelanjutan dalam pembelajaran matematika sebagai bagian dari transformasi digital di lingkungan sekolah.

items.title: Tricky trade-offs on a transparency spectrum: how the Financial Times approaches transparency about AI use in news
items.abstract: As news organisations adopt artificial intelligence (AI), they face growing pressure to be transparent about when and how it is used—yet practical approaches remain uneven. This paper examines AI transparency through an in-depth case study of the Financial Times (FT). Drawing on 13 semi-structured interviews with 12 senior managers across editorial, product, data science, and communications, together with internal documents, we show that the FT approaches transparency as a hybrid of policy, process, and practice, framed by a desire to safeguard both internal and external trust. Transparency is calibrated to context: internally, AI use is signposted in tools and reinforced through training and personal accountability; externally, the prominence of disclosure scales with system autonomy and editorial oversight, with stronger labelling for no-human-in-the-loop features than for AI-assisted, journalist-edited outputs. We identify nine factors that shape audience-facing disclosure—legal/provider requirements, industry benchmarking, nature of the task, human oversight, system novelty, audience expectations, perceived risk, commercial sensitivities, and design constraints—and five crosscutting challenges, including site-wide consistency (especially on mobile) and potential “transparency backfire.” Conceptually, our analysis links AI transparency to isomorphic pressures and to intersecting institutional logics. We argue that AI transparency in news is best understood as a spectrum, evolving with technological advancements, commercial, professional and ethical considerations and shifting audience attitudes.

items.title: Understanding Consumer Behavior Through AI-Driven Predictive Analytics
items.abstract: Abstract: The rapid proliferation of artificial intelligence (AI) and big data analytics has fundamentally transformed how organizations understand, predict, and influence consumer behavior. Despite the growing adoption of AI-driven predictive analytics in marketing, there remains limited theoretical integration explaining how these technologies shape consumer decision-making processes. This paper presents a conceptual framework that examines the relationships among AI-based personalization, predictive analytics capability, consumer data quality, and AI recommendation accuracy as independent variables, consumer trust as a mediator, and purchase intention and customer loyalty as dependent variables. Drawing upon the Technology Acceptance Model, the Theory of Planned Behavior, the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, and Expectation Confirmation Theory, the study synthesizes current literature across AI in marketing, machine learning applications, recommendation systems, customer segmentation, and consumer journey analytics. The proposed framework contributes to the literature by providing a holistic theoretical model that bridges the gap between technological capabilities and behavioral outcomes. Practical implications suggest that organizations should prioritize data quality and algorithmic transparency to foster consumer trust, while ethical considerations regarding privacy and bias in AI models warrant careful governance. The findings offer actionable insights for marketers, technology developers, and policymakers seeking to leverage predictive analytics responsibly in consumer-facing applications.

items.title: What Must Remain Human? Rethinking Business Education for 2030: A Collective Article by the Business Physics AI Lab
items.abstract: Abstract: Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) can now produce market analyses, forecasts, and client presentations in minutes. Polished output therefore reveals little about what a business student understands. This conceptual article asks which human capabilities business education must deliberately develop by 2030 so that AI extends professional competence while judgment, agency, and responsibility stay with the person. Sixteen members of the Business Physics AI Simulation Lab answered this question from their own fields, which include agentic AI, AI reliability, market research, analytics, leadership, public relations, project management, cybersecurity, and marketing automation. Two AI agents also responded. A synthesis of the eighteen perspectives identifies six capabilities: accountability and oversight; independent thinking and problem framing; evidence, verification, and critical evaluation; human communication and relationships; professional agency and resilience; and AI and technical literacy. All six rest on knowledge of the field and experience of doing the work. Ten patterns recur across the contributions, most often that foundations must come before delegation and that oversight should be proportional to risk. The article introduces the principle of safety of learning by design, and proposes four levels of human responsibility (Must Perform, Must Understand, Must Verify, Must Own) for deciding how AI should enter a learning activity. It applies the REACT framework (Reason, Evidence, Accountability, Constraints, Trade-offs) as a decision habit for students. Ten recommendations for business programs follow, including assessing judgment alongside output and making resource awareness part of AI judgment. The article argues that the goal is human-AI complementarity.

items.title: Whose Goals? Autotelic Agents Generate Goals Within Spaces They Are Given: The Goal Space and the Referee Stay Outside the Agent, and a Foundation Model in the Loop Relocates Them Rather Than Removing Them
items.abstract: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Autotelic agents are described as learning to represent, generate, select and solve their own goals, and a new generation of systems built on foundation models is reported to do so without hand-coded goal representations, without human intervention, or from zero data. This paper separates four things that the phrase "the agent generates its own goals" bundles together: the goal space in which any goal can be expressed, the selector that decides which goal to pursue next, the success test that decides whether a goal was reached, and the referee that decides whether the goals produced were new or worth having. An audit of 28 published systems and system families, from engineered-goal-space robotics to language-model task proposers, records where each component sits. The referee is outside the agent in all of them, but that is structural rather than a finding: a published evaluation is by definition its authors'. The substantive results concern the other three. The selector is computed by the agent in all 28. The goal space is written by the designers in the engineered systems and learned from designer-chosen data or objectives in the learned-space systems. In every foundation-model system it is bounded, on top of what pretraining makes available, by something the designers wrote or chose: a prompt, a seed list, an output format, a task-type menu, a simulator or the environment itself. The success test is supplied in about half of the rows (at least 13 of the 28), and where it is the model's own, the two systems that measured it against an external reference found it less accurate on later or harder self-generated goals. Where goals leave the region occupied by human examples, human raters score them as less understandable and less human-like, though the published analysis cannot separate a referee that fails to credit new goals from a generator that produces worse ones. The published ablations show that the designer-held components are not inert, but they do not rank them above the self-directed ones: in Absolute Zero, removing two designer-chosen task types and replacing the proposer's own earlier tasks with a fixed prompt cost comparable amounts, and the LMA3 comparison is qualitative. A foundation model in the loop moves the space and the referee from the designer's grammar into a pretraining corpus and a prompt; it does not remove them. On present evidence, the foundation-model systems generate goals within a supplied space, which is Sigaud et al.'s first-order open-ended case, and the tests that would support a second-order reading have not been run.

items.title: “Can you hear me, ChatGPT?”: interaction patterns, challenges, and learner perceptions in out-of-class EFL speaking practice
items.abstract: Abstract As Generative AI (GenAI) expands voice interaction capabilities, it offers new possibilities for foreign language speaking practice in more realistic interactional environments. This study investigates EFL learners’ interaction patterns with ChatGPT as an out-of-class language partner and examines how these patterns and learner perceptions evolve over time. Over a 15-week semester, thirty EFL students at a Japanese university used their smartphones to converse with ChatGPT on six designated topics. Data were collected through recordings, transcripts, and pre- and post-surveys. Content analysis revealed that students relied mainly on reactive strategies, mostly responding to ChatGPT’s questions, while demonstrating fewer proactive behaviors, such as steering the conversation or asking questions. Task design also influenced interaction patterns. Over time, increases in conversation length and proactive output suggested greater interactional engagement and growing familiarity with AI-mediated speaking practice. However, recurring technical issues, particularly interruptions, often disrupted conversational flow, leading to disengagement, as also reflected in open-ended survey responses. The tension between potential benefits and practical limitations challenges uncritical technological optimism. Although GenAI offers valuable practice opportunities, its limitations mean it complements rather than replaces human interaction. Rather than assuming technology alone transforms learning, educators must develop frameworks that address technical constraints, scaffold learner autonomy, and cultivate critical AI literacy.

items.title: A Clinician-in-the-Loop, Explainable and Fairness-Aware Framework for AI-Assisted Screening of Depression and Anxiety: Design and Validation Protocol
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) models for detecting depression and anxiety often report high accuracy in development data but rarely reach routine care, largely because of weak validation, uncalibrated outputs, opaque reasoning, unexamined bias and unclear clinical responsibility. This paper proposes a six-layer framework for AI-assisted screening of depression and anxiety that treats the model as decision support under professional oversight rather than as a diagnostic authority. The layers cover (1) ethical, consent-based multimodal data acquisition anchored on the PHQ-9, GAD-7 and a structured clinical interview; (2) quality control and preprocessing; (3) feature representation for questionnaire, clinical, language, speech and wearable data; (4) modelling with a logistic regression baseline and candidate support vector machine, random forest, gradient boosting and neural network models under nested cross-validation, calibration and external validation; (5) explanation and subgroup fairness auditing; and (6) a clinician-in-the-loop decision pathway with feedback for monitoring. A cross-cutting governance layer addresses privacy, security and accountability. A complete evaluation protocol is specified, including sample size planning, metric definitions, threshold selection and reporting under TRIPOD+AI. An analytic demonstration using published instrument accuracies shows why prevalence-aware interpretation is essential. At 5% prevalence, a screen with 0.88 sensitivity and 0.88 specificity yields a positive predictive value of only 27.8%, rising to 64.7% at 20% prevalence, while negative predictive value stays above 96%. The framework gives researchers and clinicians a reproducible template for developing, validating and deploying AI screening tools responsibly.

items.title: A Human-AI Collaborative Framework for Airport X-Ray Weapon Detection Using Deep Transfer Learning
items.abstract: This study investigates the combined impact of human factors and deep learning on weapon detection performance in airport X-ray screening. A controlled experiment with 78 participants evaluated the effects of operator motivation and screen background color on detection accuracy and response time. The results showed that motivation significantly improves accuracy and reduces response time, particularly for prohibited items, whereas background color has no measurable effect. To address human performance variability, a transfer learning–based detection framework using SE-ResNet-50 was developed, achieving 98.87% accuracy and surpassing existing benchmarks. These findings highlight that integrating human-centered design principles with Artificial Intelligence (AI)-assisted systems can enhance detection consistency and reliability, offering actionable insights for operational airport security and the design of future AI-human collaborative systems.

items.title: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for LLM-Driven Task Planning and Execution in Industrial Assembly
items.abstract: This paper proposes a neuro-symbolic framework that combines large language model (LLM)-driven task planning with formal symbolic verification and reactive Behavior Tree execution to support high-precision operations in industrial assembly. While Large Language Models (LLMs) demonstrate expertise in interpreting natural language instructions, they often struggle with processing structured manufacturing data and lack long-horizon planning capabilities and deterministic physical awareness required for complex robotic execution. Furthermore, their susceptibility to generating physically unfeasible sequences and their lack of robust error-recovery mechanisms limit their autonomous deployment. To address these limitations, the proposed pipeline decomposes the assembly process into sequential stages of planning, technological grounding, adaptive execution, and recovery. Initially, the framework leverages LLMs to synthesize multi-modal inputs—ranging from natural language directives to formalized product and process specifications—into a formal Hierarchical Task Network (HTN). To ensure physical feasibility, a deterministic rule-based compiler validates the HTN’s syntactic and structural consistency, rejecting undefined symbols and non-decomposable tasks, against established spatial and operational constraints. This verified logical sequence is subsequently compiled into a reactive Behavior Tree (BT) that guides execution through a fixed robotic skill library. During execution, a real-time object detection system and an atomic skill library dynamically translate the BT into grounded actions. Designed for human–robot collaborative environments, the architecture autonomously allocates standard operations to the robotic agent while safely deferring tasks requiring high dexterity to human operators. By combining the semantic adaptability of LLMs with the rigorous state validation of deterministic rule-based tools, this methodology is intended to reduce hallucination-driven failures and support safer manufacturing workflows, as evaluated through a system-level feasibility study rather than a component-wise ablation. The proposed architecture is evaluated against both physical and logical criteria using task-specific evaluation metrics. The framework was evaluated on four assembly tasks (T1–T4) using two Gemma model configurations, with 30 trials per task for each configuration (120 trials per configuration; 240 trials in total), achieving near-100% plan validity and near-zero hallucination rates under the higher-capacity configuration. Future integration of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) policies at the level of individual Behavior Tree leaves is discussed in Section Perception and Dynamic Adaptation as a promising direction to replace the current fixed robotic skill set.
